svg.title: Follow-up schedules for three tumours, and how the method of measurement decides the answer to "has it grown"
svg.desc: Schematic on the follow-up schedules for three benign brain tumours and on how the method of measurement decides the answer to "has it grown". The first section shows three guidelines as three deliberately unaligned schedules, with a rule between them marked "not aligned; not interchangeable". The meningioma axis comes from the EANO 2021 guideline at the level of a good clinical practice statement, that is, expert consensus, quoted as: "currently, by consensus, for a suspected meningioma or a grade 1 meningioma, annual MRI for five years is recommended; thereafter intervals may be doubled", with years 1 to 5 marked on the axis and "intervals may then be doubled" at its end. The vestibular schwannoma axis comes from the CNS 2018 imaging guideline as a level 3 recommendation, the lowest, quoted as: "MRI should be performed annually for five years; thereafter the interval may be lengthened provided the tumour is stable", with a note that an updated version appeared in 2026 with different wording and different intervals. The pituitary adenoma axis comes from the Endocrine Society 2011 incidentaloma guideline, for incidentalomas that do not meet the surgical criteria, quoted as: "MRI at 6 months for a macroadenoma and at one year for a microadenoma, with intervals lengthened stepwise thereafter if the size is unchanged; visual field testing at 6 months and annually for those whose lesion abuts or compresses the optic nerves and chiasm; endocrine testing at 6 months and annually for a macroadenoma". The figure states the level of evidence plainly: the meningioma line is expert consensus; every relevant recommendation in the vestibular schwannoma guideline set is level 3, and its authors write in their executive summary that "several well-designed questions and subsequent searches did not yield information sufficient to make meaningful and supportable recommendations"; there is no randomised trial behind these intervals, and the doctor adjusts them to the patient. The second section puts two meningioma numbers in the same frame to show that changing the ruler reverses the answer. On the left, measured by volume: Behbahani 2019, a prospective study of 64 people with an incidental meningioma followed for five years, with growth defined as 15% more volume than baseline, found 75% — that is, 48 tumours — increased in volume; the same study reports five growth patterns of which the S-shaped one accounts for 35% and more than six in ten are self-limiting, so projecting this year's rate ten years ahead is wrong as a method, and growth rate varies with age at 0.10 cm³ a year under 55, 0.24 from 55 to 75 and 0.85 over 75. On the right, a composite progression endpoint: the IMPACT external validation in JAMA Oncology 2026, covering 1,248 people and 1,010 untreated meningiomas across 33 centres in 15 countries with median follow-up of 61 months, defines the endpoint as growth, or symptoms, or meningioma-related death, or loss of the window for cure, and reports 85.7% progression-free at ten years and 88.1% at five; in the same cohort 383 people (40.5%) died of something else with the meningioma quiet and untreated. The figure states that three-quarters growing and 85.7% not progressing at ten years are true at the same time, so the correct sentence is "most will not come to harm from it", stated together with which ruler was used. A further note records that a meta-analysis of 20 studies and 2,130 people, with its 2019 correction, found 8.4% developing symptoms during active monitoring (95% confidence interval 2.8 to 16.7%) and 24.8% going on to an intervention, and that most patients who progressed did so within five years of diagnosis. The third section is headed that for vestibular schwannoma, observation is paid for in hearing. Kirchmann 2017 followed 156 intracanalicular vestibular schwannomas managed conservatively for a mean of 9.5 years: the pure tone average worsened from 51 dB to 72 dB, the word recognition score fell from 60% to 34%, the proportion with AAO-HNS class A hearing fell from 19% to 3%, tumour growth occurred in 37% and conservative management failed in 15%. In the same 156 people at the same follow-up, changing the scoring system moves the answer by 24 percentage points: serviceable hearing was preserved in 34% scored by AAO-HNS classes A and B, and in 58% scored by word recognition score classes 1 and 2. The figure draws these two as bars side by side and notes that it is the same people at the same follow-up with only the scoring system changed, so whenever a "preservation rate" appears, the first question is which ruler it used. The CNS hearing-preservation guideline puts the probability of retaining serviceable hearing in the observation group at greater than 75% to 100% at year 2, greater than 50% to 75% at year 5 and greater than 25% to 50% at year 10, and adds that the most consistent predictors are hearing before treatment and the absence of tumour growth. For vestibular schwannoma, growth means 2 mm more in maximum diameter: of 3,637 sporadic vestibular schwannomas in Denmark between 1976 and 2015, 2,312 people were observed for a mean of 7.33 years, with growth defined as an increase in linear measurement of more than 2 mm following the Tokyo 2001 consensus; split by site, 21% of intracanalicular tumours and 37% of those extending into the cerebellopontine angle had grown by five years after diagnosis, and 25% and 42% by ten years, with growth occurring mainly within the first five years, and 434 people (19%) moving to active treatment because of growth. "It has grown" is not "it will keep growing": a four-centre study of 592 people who kept being observed after growth had been measured found that, counting from the first detection of growth, 32% of intracanalicular tumours and 22% of cerebellopontine angle tumours had not grown again within five years, and the authors conclude that growth detected during observation does not necessarily predict future growth and that tolerating some growth is defensible in appropriately selected patients — a qualifier that cannot be dropped, since who is appropriately selected is the doctor's choice. The fourth section states that for pituitary adenoma observation measures three things, and that the ruler changes again to an event rate per 100 person-years: macroadenoma 12.5 per 100 person-years (95% confidence interval 7.9 to 17.2), solid lesions 5.7, microadenoma 3.3, new endocrine dysfunction overall 2.4, and cystic lesions 0.05. The source is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies with follow-up of three to fifteen years; pituitary apoplexy and worsening visual field defects were both rare; the authors rate the quality of this evidence as very low and record marked heterogeneity. Observation of a pituitary adenoma is not imaging alone — the same guideline requires visual field and endocrine testing as well. The fifth section covers what stops observation and what loosens follow-up. For meningioma: "symptomatic or growing". For vestibular schwannoma: once growth is measured, sorted by site, with intracanalicular tumours mostly kept under observation and those extending into the cerebellopontine angle mostly going to surgery. For pituitary adenoma: the Endocrine Society surgical list — a visual field defect, visual abnormality or neurological compromise from compression, a lesion abutting the visual pathway, pituitary apoplexy with visual disturbance, or a hypersecreting tumour other than a prolactinoma. On loosening, the meningioma column has a study: a prognostic model of 441 people shows that after five years of follow-up the risk of progression plateaus in every risk group, and that people with an age-adjusted Charlson comorbidity index of 6 or more, an 80-year-old with chronic kidney disease for example, are 15 times more likely to die of another cause than to receive an intervention within five years of diagnosis, regardless of risk group. But none of the three guidelines states a number of unchanged years after which follow-up can stop. The figure records that this is a decision the doctor makes after stratifying with a tool and is not the patient's to make, and that the question worth asking in clinic is which tool was used and which items were looked at to put them in that layer. The sixth section covers Taiwan, drawn as three gates. Gate 1, is your tumour in the indications: the indications for items 37028B and 37029B of the payment schedule do list "acoustic neuroma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, craniopharyngioma". Gate 2, and one of the following conditions must be met: "A. has had a craniotomy but has residual or recurrent tumour. B. craniotomy would risk neurological injury or carries high risk. C. has severe cardiopulmonary or other medical disease making invasive surgery or general anaesthesia unsuitable. … F. a unilateral intracranial cerebellopontine angle acoustic neuroma less than 2.5 cm in width (excluding the internal auditory canal)." Gate 3, every case requires prior case-by-case application to the insurer, word for word from the regulation, with no exception. The exit reads: in plain words, the regulation places radiosurgery after "surgery is not an option or is too risky", not first, which is why the first step in Taiwan is so often observation or surgery. As for how often follow-up MRI is covered, there is no line item for these three tumours anywhere in the schedule — and no line item is not the same as not covered; how to code and claim it is a question for the hospital's medical affairs office. The figure closes on the reading that is ruled out: it does not say "everyone gets observed anyway". Observation is not doing nothing and it is not one prescription shared by three diseases, and the three schedules are deliberately not aligned precisely to block carrying one of them across to another. A growth rate is not a guarantee: every "growth" above is tied to one way of measuring — maximum diameter or volume, a linear measurement or a composite endpoint — and with the label stripped off the numbers cannot be compared. Before leaving the clinic, fill in four boxes: the month of the next scan and which sequence; what is to be measured alongside it, that is hearing, visual fields and hormone blood tests; which situations mean coming back early, asked of the doctor for that tumour specifically; and today's measurement — how many millimetres in maximum diameter or how many cubic centimetres in volume, and by which method.

g.text: OBSERVATION IS A PRESCRIPTION, NOT A PAUSE
Three schedules, deliberately not aligned
Observation is a prescription: a named scan, an interval, things to be measured alongside it, and written stopping conditions. The
prescription is different for each of the three.
And the question "has it grown" reverses when you change the ruler — so every number here is labelled with how it was measured.
Three guidelines, three different schedules
The three axes are deliberately not aligned, because they are not aligned. The level of evidence follows each one.
meningioma
EANO 2021 guideline

The level of evidence has to be stated plainly: the meningioma line is expert consensus; every relevant recommendation in the vestibular schwannoma guideline set is level 3, the
lowest, and its authors write in their executive summary that "several well-designed questions and subsequent searches did not yield information sufficient to make meaningful and
supportable recommendations". There is no randomised trial behind these intervals, and your doctor will adjust them to your situation.
Meningioma: change the ruler and the answer reverses
These two numbers belong in the same frame. They do not conflict — what conflicts is the definition of "growth".
measured by volume
Behbahani 2019 (prospective study)
n=64 people with an incidental meningioma, followed for five years
growth defined as: 15% more volume than baseline
48 tumours increased in volume
From the same study: there are five growth patterns, of which the S-shaped one
accounts for 35%, and more than six in ten are self-limiting — so projecting this year's
rate ten years ahead is wrong as a method. Growth rate varies with age: 0.10 cm³ a
year under 55, 0.24 from 55 to 75 and 0.85 over 75.
composite progression endpoint
IMPACT external validation (JAMA Oncology 2026)
1,248 people and 1,010 untreated meningiomas across 33 centres in 15 countries, median
follow-up 61 months

of the window for cure
progression-free at ten years (88.1% at five years)
In the same cohort, 383 people (40.5%) died of something else with the meningioma
quiet and untreated. Older people grow them faster, and older people are also
likeliest to leave first for another reason — the two sentences are only complete
together.
Three-quarters growing, and 85.7% not progressing at ten years, are true at the same time. So the correct sentence is "most will not come to harm from it", stated together with
which ruler was used.
Does observing let things slip? A meta-analysis of 20 studies and 2,130 people, with its 2019 correction, gives this: 8.4% developed symptoms during active monitoring (95% confidence
interval 2.8 to 16.7%) and 24.8% went on to have an intervention; "most patients who progressed did so within five years of diagnosis".
For vestibular schwannoma, observation is paid for in hearing
The same 156 people, the same follow-up — change the scoring system and the answer moves by 24 percentage points.
vestibular schwannoma
Kirchmann 2017: 156 intracanalicular vestibular schwannomas managed conservatively, mean follow-up 9.5 years

Same people, same follow-up, only a different scoring system. So whenever you meet a "preservation rate", ask first: which ruler is that?
CNS hearing-preservation guideline: probability of retaining serviceable hearing in the observation group (vestibular schwannoma)
year 2

It adds that the most consistent predictors are hearing before treatment and the absence of tumour growth.
For vestibular schwannoma, "growth" is 2 mm more in maximum diameter
Of 3,637 sporadic vestibular schwannomas in Denmark between 1976 and 2015, 2,312 people were observed, with a mean follow-up of 7.33 years; growth was defined as "an
increase in linear measurement of more than 2 mm", following the Tokyo 2001 consensus. Split by site, the proportion that had grown by five years after diagnosis was 21% for
intracanalicular tumours and 37% for those extending into the cerebellopontine angle, and by ten years 25% and 42%, with growth occurring "mainly within the first five years". 434
people (19%) moved to active treatment because of growth.
"It has grown" is not "it will keep growing". A four-centre study of 592 people who kept being observed after growth had been measured found that, counting from the first
detection of growth, 32% of intracanalicular tumours and 22% of cerebellopontine angle tumours had not grown again within five years; the authors conclude that "growth detected
during observation does not necessarily predict future growth… tolerating some growth is defensible in appropriately selected patients". That qualifier cannot be dropped: who is
appropriately selected is the doctor's choice.
For pituitary adenoma, observation measures three things
The ruler changes again here: this one is an event rate per 100 person-years.

The source is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies with follow-up of three to fifteen years; pituitary apoplexy and worsening visual field defects were both rare.
The authors rate the quality of this body of evidence as "very low" and record marked heterogeneity.
Observation of a pituitary adenoma is not imaging alone: the same guideline requires visual field and endocrine testing as well.
What stops observation, and what loosens follow-up
meningioma
"symptomatic or growing".
vestibular schwannoma
once growth is measured, sorted by site: intracanalicular tumours are mostly kept under observation, those extending into the cerebellopontine
angle mostly go to surgery.
pituitary adenoma
the Endocrine Society surgical list: a visual field defect, visual abnormality or neurological compromise from compression, a lesion abutting the visual
pathway, pituitary apoplexy with visual disturbance, or a hypersecreting tumour other than a prolactinoma.
On loosening, the meningioma column has a study: a prognostic model of 441 people shows that after five years of follow-up the risk of progression plateaus in every risk group;
and that people with an age-adjusted Charlson comorbidity index of 6 or more (an 80-year-old with chronic kidney disease, say) are "15 times more likely to die of another cause
than to receive an intervention within five years of diagnosis, regardless of risk group". But none of the three guidelines states a number of unchanged years after which follow-up
can stop.
This is a decision the doctor makes after stratifying with a tool; it is not yours to make. The question worth asking in clinic is: which tool did you use, and
which items did you look at, to put me in this layer?
In Taiwan, stereotactic radiosurgery is not the default first route
Quoted from the regulation and drawn as gates: all three must be passed before an application is even possible.
Gate 1: is your tumour in the indications
The indications for items 37028B and 37029B of the payment schedule do list "acoustic neuroma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, craniopharyngioma".
Gate 2: and one of the following conditions must be met
"A. has had a craniotomy but has residual or recurrent tumour. B. craniotomy would risk neurological injury or carries high risk. C. has severe cardiopulmonary or
other medical disease making invasive surgery or general anaesthesia unsuitable. … F. a unilateral intracranial cerebellopontine angle acoustic neuroma less than 2.5
cm in width (excluding the internal auditory canal)."
Gate 3: every case requires prior case-by-case application to the insurer
Word for word from the regulation. There is no exception to this one.
In plain words: the regulation places radiosurgery after "surgery is not an option or is too risky", not first. That is why the first step in Taiwan is so often
observation or surgery.
As for how often follow-up MRI is covered, there is no line item for these three tumours anywhere in the schedule — and no line item is not the same as not covered. How to code
and claim it is a question for the hospital's medical affairs office.
This figure does not say "everyone gets observed anyway"
Observation is not doing nothing, and it is not one prescription shared by three diseases. The three schedules are deliberately not aligned precisely to block
carrying one of them across to another.
A growth rate is not a guarantee. Every "growth" above is tied to one way of measuring — maximum diameter or volume, a linear measurement or a composite
endpoint — and with the label stripped off the numbers cannot be compared.
Before leaving the clinic, fill in four boxes: the month of the next scan and which sequence; what is to be measured alongside it (hearing, visual fields, hormone
blood tests); which situations mean coming back early, asked of your doctor for your tumour specifically; and today's measurement — how many millimetres in
maximum diameter or how many cubic centimetres in volume, and by which method.
Schematic, redrawn from the EANO 2021 meningioma guideline, the CNS 2018 imaging guideline and its executive summary, the Endocrine Society 2011 pituitary
incidentaloma guideline, Behbahani 2019, the IMPACT external validation (JAMA Oncology 2026), the Islim 2019 meta-analysis with its 2019 correction, Reznitsky 2021,
Marinelli 2021, Kirchmann 2017, the CNS 2018 hearing-preservation guideline, Fernández-Balsells 2011, Islim 2020, and Taiwan's National Health Insurance payment schedule
and medical expense review guidance, rather than reproduced from their figures; the cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying sources differ, so the data points must
not be compared directly.
